turns.prompt_text: Using fish terminal on mac, how can I make an alias that also takes an input boolean
turns.response_html:
In the Fish shell, standard aliases are just shortcuts for simple commands. If you want to include logic—like handling a boolean input—you actually want to create a function.

Fish handles functions beautifully, and they are the preferred way to do anything more complex than a basic one-liner.

1. The Function Syntax

Instead of alias, you define a function that checks the first argument ($argv[1]) passed to it.

Here is a template you can copy into your terminal to test:

function toggle_mode
    if test "$argv[1]" = "true"
        echo "System set to ON"
        # Run your 'true' commands here
    else
        echo "System set to OFF"
        # Run your 'false' commands here
    end
end

2. A Practical Example (Git Push)

Let’s say you want a command gp (git push) that takes a boolean to decide whether to use the --force flag.

function gp
    if test "$argv[1]" = "true"
        git push --force
        echo "Pushing with force! 🚀"
    else
        git push
        echo "Standard push completed."
    end
end

Usage:

  • gp true → Pushes with force.
  • gp false (or anything else) → Pushes normally.

3. How to Make it Permanent

In Fish, you don't need to manually edit a .bashrc or .zshrc file every time. You have two easy options:

Option A: The "Fish Way" (Recommended)

After you’ve typed your function into the terminal and verified it works, simply run:

funcsave function_name

This automatically creates a file at ~/.config/fish/functions/function_name.fish, making it available every time you open a new window.

Option B: The Config File

If you prefer keeping everything in one place, you can paste the function code into your config file:

  1. Open the config: nano ~/.config/fish/config.fish
  2. Paste the function at the bottom.
  3. Save and exit.

Pro-Tip: Handling "Truthy" Values

If you want your "boolean" to be a bit more flexible (accepting 1, y, or true), you can use a switch statement instead:

function my_command
    switch "$argv[1]"
        case true y 1
            echo "Proceeding..."
        case "*"
            echo "Aborting."
    end
end

What specific command or workflow are you trying to automate with this boolean?

turns.prompt_text: In the fish terminal, can the ~/.config/fish/config.fish file find all sub-folders of the /functions folder to load all sub-functions?
turns.response_html:
By default, the Fish shell only looks directly inside ~/.config/fish/functions/ for .fish files. It does not automatically recurse into sub-folders.

However, you can easily tell Fish to look into those subdirectories by updating the $fish_function_path variable in your config.fish file.

The Solution

Add this snippet to your ~/.config/fish/config.fish file. This code finds all sub-directories within your functions folder and adds them to the path Fish uses to look up commands:

# Add all subdirectories of the functions folder to the function path
if test -d ~/.config/fish/functions
    set -l subdirs (find ~/.config/fish/functions -type d)
    set fish_function_path $subdirs $fish_function_path
end

How it Works

  1. find ~/.config/fish/functions -type d: This command lists the main functions folder and every folder inside it.
  2. set -l subdirs: This stores that list of folders into a local variable.
  3. set fish_function_path $subdirs $fish_function_path: This prepends those new directories to the existing function path.

Why do this?

  • Organization: You can group your scripts by category (e.g., functions/git/, functions/docker/, functions/utils/).
  • Lazy Loading: Fish is smart. It doesn't actually "load" the code until you type the command. By adding the folders to the path, you're just telling Fish, "If you don't recognize a command, check these folders too."
  • Performance: Because Fish only loads functions when they are called, having hundreds of files in sub-folders won't slow down your terminal's startup time.

A Note on Performance

If you have a massive number of nested folders, using find on every shell startup can technically add a few milliseconds of delay. If you notice a lag (which is unlikely on a modern Mac), you could hard-code the paths instead:

set fish_function_path ~/.config/fish/functions/git ~/.config/fish/functions/work $fish_function_path

Are you planning on organizing a large library of custom scripts, or just looking to keep your main config file clean?

turns.prompt_text: How can I synchronize my fish config and functions across both my mac mini and mac air?
turns.response_html:
Synchronizing your setup between two Macs is a rite of passage for power users. Since Fish stores almost everything in ~/.config/fish, you have a few solid paths depending on how much manual control you want.

Method 1: The Git Approach (Professional & Safe)

This is the "gold standard." You treat your configuration like a software project. It gives you a history of changes, so if you break a function on your Air, you can revert it from your Mini.

  1. Initialize on Mac 1: 
    cd ~/.config/fish
git init
git add .
git commit -m "Initial fish config sync"
  2. Push to a Private Repo: Create a private repository on GitHub or GitLab and push your code there.
  3. Clone on Mac 2: On your second Mac, back up your existing fish folder, then clone: 
    mv ~/.config/fish ~/.config/fish_backup
git clone [your-repo-url] ~/.config/fish
  4. Workflow: When you change a function, just git commit and git push. On the other machine, run git pull.

Method 2: iCloud or Dropbox (Set-it-and-forget-it)

If you don't want to deal with "pushing" and "pulling" code, you can use symlinks to trick Fish into reading from your cloud storage.

  1. Move the folder to the cloud: 
    mv ~/.config/fish ~/Library/Mobile\ Documents/com~apple~CloudDocs/fish_sync
  2. Create a Symlink: On both Macs, link the expected location to the cloud location: 
    ln -s ~/Library/Mobile\ Documents/com~apple~CloudDocs/fish_sync ~/.config/fish

    Warning: Cloud syncing can sometimes cause "file conflicts" if you have the terminal open on both machines and change settings simultaneously.

Method 3: Mackup (The Automated Way)

Mackup is a popular CLI tool specifically designed to back up and sync application settings (including Fish) using Dropbox, iCloud, or Git.

  1. Install it: brew install mackup
  2. Configure it: Create a .mackup.cfg file in your home directory: 
    [storage]
engine = icloud
  3. Run it:
    • On the first Mac: mackup backup (This moves your config to the cloud and leaves a symlink behind).
    • On the second Mac: mackup restore (This replaces the local config with a symlink to the cloud).

⚠️ Important: Handling Machine-Specific Configs

Since you are syncing between a Mini (desktop) and an Air (laptop), you might want different settings for each (e.g., a specific monitor setup or battery-saving aliases).

To handle this, keep your config.fish synced but add this logic to the bottom of the file:

# Check the hostname and load a local file if it exists
set -l host_config ~/.config/fish/config.(hostname).fish
if test -f $host_config
    source $host_config
end

Then, create config.MacMini.fish and config.MacAir.fish for settings that shouldn't be shared.

Which of these sounds more like your style—the manual control of Git or the "invisible" sync of iCloud?

turns.prompt_text: would if I host it on icloud, but also keep git for history
turns.response_html:
This hybrid approach is actually a very popular "set-it-and-forget-it" strategy. It gives you the instant syncing of iCloud with the safety net of Git history.

How the Hybrid Setup Works

You will essentially store the "Source of Truth" in iCloud, track it with Git there, and then "point" your Macs to that folder using a symlink.

Step-by-Step Implementation

1. Move and Link (On Mac #1)

First, move your existing configuration into your iCloud Drive and create the connection.

# 1. Move the folder to iCloud
mv ~/.config/fish ~/Library/Mobile\ Documents/com~apple~CloudDocs/fish_dotfiles

# 2. Create the symlink so Fish can still find it
ln -s ~/Library/Mobile\ Documents/com~apple~CloudDocs/fish_dotfiles ~/.config/fish

2. Initialize Git (In the iCloud folder)

Now, turn that iCloud folder into a Git repository.

cd ~/Library/Mobile\ Documents/com~apple~CloudDocs/fish_dotfiles
git init
git add .
git commit -m "Initial setup with iCloud sync"

3. Connect Mac #2

On your second machine, you just need to delete the local (empty) fish folder and point it to the one iCloud just finished downloading.

# Remove the default folder
rm -rf ~/.config/fish

# Link to the iCloud folder
ln -s ~/Library/Mobile\ Documents/com~apple~CloudDocs/fish_dotfiles ~/.config/fish

⚠️ The "Conflict" Warning

iCloud and Git don't always play nice because the .git folder contains hundreds of tiny files that change every time you commit.

  • The Risk: If both Macs are online and you perform a Git operation, iCloud might try to sync a file while Git is writing to it, leading to a "Duplicate File" or "Conflict" error inside your .git folder.
  • The Fix: Only run Git commands (commit, branch, etc.) from one machine at a time. Once you commit on the Mini, wait a few seconds for the "Cloud" icon in Finder to finish before doing work on the Air.

A Cleaner Alternative: The "Bare" Repo

If you want to avoid the iCloud conflict risk entirely while still using Git, many developers use a Bare Repository. This keeps your config files in their natural place (~/.config/fish) but tracks them in a hidden folder elsewhere.

Would you like to see how to set up a "Bare" Git repo, or does the iCloud symlink feel like the right level of simplicity for you?
